title: METR Time Horizons and External Capability Evaluation

questions.question: A model succeeds more often on short expert tasks and less often as task duration increases. How can a single time-horizon number summarize that curve?
options: Use the average prompt length in the evaluation set
Use the expert task duration where fitted success is 50 percent
Use the longest task with one successful run
Use the task duration where success first reaches 100 percent
questions.explanation: The horizon is the expert task duration where a fitted success-versus-log-time curve reaches 50%. The longest task with one successful run ignores repeated reliability and the rest of the fitted curve.

questions.question: What is the fitting target in the METR time-horizon method described here?
options: Number of tokens as a function of model release date
Task cost as a function of agent count
Human preference as a function of output length
Success probability as a function of log expert completion time
questions.explanation: METR fits task-success probability as a function of log expert completion time, then finds its 50% crossing. Release date, task cost, and human preference are different variables, not the fit target.

questions.question: Why does the lesson call benchmark horizons upper bounds on deployment capability?
options: Benchmarks always include harder tasks than any production workflow
The fit intentionally reports the lowest possible success rate
Benchmarks use idealized tools and omit real consequences and user variation
Deployment tasks are all shorter than benchmark tasks
questions.explanation: Benchmarks use cleaner tools and prompts, omit real consequences, and do not reproduce user variation or deployment context. Those differences can lower real reliability; benchmarks do not necessarily use harder tasks or report a minimum.

questions.question: A model appears unusually successful when it can infer it is in an evaluation. What can this do to the observed horizon?
options: Inflate success observations and shift the fitted horizon upward
Force the fitted curve to be independent of task duration
Make the expert-time axis equal to wall-clock deployment time
Lower all observed success rates by the gaming rate
questions.explanation: The simulator flips some failures into observed successes; that lifts the fitted success curve and can move the horizon upward. Gaming does not make success independent of task duration.

questions.question: A vendor claims a long time horizon, but your proposed task uses unfamiliar tools and has real consequences. What is the sound next step?
options: Skip evaluation because the horizon is already expressed in hours
Treat the vendor horizon as an autonomous deployment guarantee
Use only the benchmark's easiest tasks to confirm the claim
Run an evaluation on your own representative task distribution
questions.explanation: Run a representative evaluation with your own tools, consequences, and task mix because vendor benchmark conditions do not automatically match deployment. A number expressed in hours is not a production guarantee.

questions.question: A proposed task requires substantially longer expert work than the model's measured horizon. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Assume the model will succeed because one benchmark task ran long
Replace external measurement with the agent's self-assessment
Extend the task until the fitted horizon catches up
Do not ship it autonomously without enough margin and task-specific evaluation
questions.explanation: If the task is much longer than the measured horizon, do not deploy it autonomously without margin and task-specific evidence. One exceptional long success does not erase the fitted reliability gap.
